title: Hybrid Fuzzing with LLM-Guided Input Mutation and Semantic Feedback
authors: Shiyin Lin
abstract: Software fuzzing has become a cornerstone in automated vulnerability discovery, yet existing mutation strategies often lack semantic awareness, leading to redundant test cases and slow exploration of deep program states. In this work, we present a hybrid fuzzing framework that integrates static and dynamic analysis with Large Language Model (LLM)-guided input mutation and semantic feedback. Static analysis extracts control-flow and data-flow information, which is transformed into structured prompts for the LLM to generate syntactically valid and semantically diverse inputs. During execution, we augment traditional coverage-based feedback with semantic feedback signals—derived from program state changes, exception types, and output semantics—allowing the fuzzer to prioritize inputs that trigger novel program behaviors beyond mere code coverage. We implement our approach atop AFL++, combining program instrumentation with embedding-based semantic similarity metrics to guide seed selection. Evaluation on real-world open-source targets, including libpng, tcpdump, and sqlite, demonstrates that our method achieves faster time-to-first-bug, higher semantic diversity, and a competitive number of unique bugs compared to state-of-the-art fuzzers. This work highlights the potential of combining LLM reasoning with semantic-aware feedback to accelerate and deepen vulnerability discovery.

title: Does the Verdict Function Matter? How Evaluation Rewards Causally Steer Automated LLM Fuzzing and Distort Discovered Vulnerabilities
authors: Ashish Vishwakarma
abstract: When security teams run automated red-teaming fuzzers against Large Language Models (LLMs), an automated verdict function acts as the reward signal guiding the search algorithm. While recent studies have examined static differences between scoring metrics, an essential question remains unaddressed: How does the choice of verdict function causally steer what an active adversarial search algorithm discovers and misses? In this paper, we run a controlled experiment showing that the verdict function acts as an active steering wheel rather than a passive scoreboard. Holding the target model (Qwen2-57B-A14B-Instruct), the search algorithm (UCB-1 bandit fuzzer), the mutation operators, and query budgets strictly invariant, we evaluate five canonical verdict functions: refusal-prefix matching (𝑉 1), keyword blocklists (𝑉 2), LLM-as-a-judge (𝑉 3), lexical intent preservation (𝑉 4), and multi-objective combined scoring (𝑉 5). Our investigation establishes four primary findings: (1) Causal Search Steering &amp; Policy Collapse (Headline Finding): When guided by refusal-prefix matching (𝑉 1), the multi-armed bandit fuzzer rapidly collapses into selecting superficial conversational wrappers (38.6%). The set of successful jailbreak prompts discovered under 𝑉 1 shares only a 12.0% Jaccard overlap (𝐽 = 0.120) with those discovered under multi-objective guidance (𝑉 5). (2) Search Blindness to Real Vulnerabilities: Because prefix matching rewards non-refusal conversational fillers, the fuzzer spends its query budget harvesting superficial text (𝜇 = 1.42/5.0 relevance), remaining systematically blind to over 85% of the actionable jailbreak vectors discovered under semantic guidance. (3) Massive Reporting Divergence (Δ &gt; 50%): On identical model responses from Qwen2-57B, prefix matching reports an Attack Success Rate (ASR) of 84.2%, compared to 31.8% under combined evaluation (𝑝 = 1.83 × 10-10 under McNemar's test). (4) Downstream Defense Contamination: Defensive activation probes trained on hard negatives mined under prefix matching suffer a 0.208 drop in test AUROC (AUROC = 0.786 vs. 0.991) because labeling errors pollute defensive training boundaries. We establish the Calibrated Dual-Verdict Protocol (CDVP) to prevent metric-induced search distortion and ensure reliable vulnerability discovery in automated red-teaming. title: Optimization Research of Directed Fuzzing Based on AFL
authors: Tao Feng; Jinkun Liu
abstract: Fuzz testing is the process of testing programs by continually producing unique inputs in order to detect and identify security flaws. It is often used in vulnerability mining. The most prevalent fuzzing approach is grey-box fuzzing, which combines lightweight code instrumentation with data-feedback-driven generation of fresh program input seeds. AFL (American Fuzzy Lop) is an outstanding grey-box fuzzing tool that is well known for its quick fork server execution, dependable genetic algorithm, and numerous mutation techniques. AFLGO proposes and executes power scheduling based on a simulated annealing process for a more appropriate energy allocation to seeds, however it is neither reliable nor successful. To tackle this issue, we offer an energy-dynamic scheduling strategy based on the algorithm of the fruit fly. Adjusting the energy of the seeds dynamically controls the production of test cases. The findings demonstrate that the approach suggested in this research can test the target region more rapidly and thoroughly and has a high application value for patch testing and vulnerability replication.

title: Constraint-Informed Directed Kernel Fuzzing for Hard-to-Reach Code Regions Authors
authors: Giulia Romano; Luca Ferraro; Marco Bianchi
abstract: In this study, we explore constraint inference to improve directed fuzzing for rarely executed kernel regions. The proposed system extracts partial symbolic constraints using lightweight solver queries and integrates them with distance-based fuzzing heuristics. Testing on 10 common Linux drivers, the fuzzer reduces target-reaching time by 63% and uncovers 6 new memory-corruption issues. Constraint caching avoids repeated solver calls and maintains throughput at 2.8k exec/s. Findings suggest that even partial constraints sharply increase efficiency in guided exploration of deep kernel logic.

title: RLTG: Multi-targets directed greybox fuzzing
authors: Yubo He; Yuefei Zhu
abstract: Directed greybox fuzzing guides fuzzers to explore specific objective code areas and has achieved good performance in some scenarios such as patch testing. However, if there are multiple objective code to explore, existing directed greybox fuzzers, such as AFLGo and Hawkeye, often neglect some targets because they use harmonic means of distance and prefers to test those targets with shorter reachable path. Besides, existing directed greybox fuzzers cannot calculate the accurate distance due to indirect calls in the program. In addition, existing directed greybox fuzzers fail to address the exploration and exploitation problem and have poor efficiency in seed scheduling. To address these problems, we propose a dynamic seed distance calculation scheme, it increase the seed distance dynamically when the reachable path encounter indirect call. Besides, the seed distance calculation can deal with the bias problem in multi-targets scenarios. With the seed distance calculation method, we propose a new seed scheduling algorithm based on the upper confidence bound algorithm to deal with the exploration and exploitation problem in drected greybox fuzzing. We implemented a prototype RLTG and evaluate it on real-world programs. Evaluation of our prototype shows that our approach outperforms a state-of-the-art directed fuzzer AFLGo. On the multi-targets benchmark Magma, RLTG reproduces bugs with 6.9x speedup and finds 66.7% more bugs than AFLGo.
